incidents.Description: Anti-Witness riot that involved the entire town and drew national attention.
incidents.Notes: ACLU 1941 pamphlet (pp. 15–16) adds detail: about 100 Witnesses arrived in 21 cars; 12 cars wrecked beyond repair, $8,000+ in damage; 64 Witnesses taken to the police station by the mob and beaten to force a flag salute while the police chief watched from his car. DOJ ordered the evidence put to a grand jury in Oct. 1940.

incidents.Description: Anti-Witness riot that involved the entire town and drew national attention.
incidents.Notes: ACLU 1941 pamphlet breaks this into individual incidents: see JW-50 to JW-57.

incidents.Description: A jeering mob drove a disheveled group of Witness men and women out of town under a hail of brick fragments and other missiles while the sheriff watched. The sheriff told journalist Beulah Amidon they were traitors because "the Supreme Court says so."
incidents.Source cited in text: Amidon, "Can We Afford Martyrs?" Survey Graphic, Sept. 1, 1940
incidents.Notes: Town and state not named in the source.

incidents.Description: A city patrolman and a deputy sheriff questioned and held three Witness women and one man after hearing they were distributing "Fifth Column stuff." After phoning the police chief, they ordered the group out of town within an hour or face charges, and said that next time they would be handed to the American Legion.
incidents.Source cited in text: Affidavit of Roy Crabb, Jan. 9, 1941, ACLUP vol. 2317
incidents.Notes: The same affiant, Roy Crabb, was beaten in Ash Fork, AZ on June 19, 1940 (JW-34).

incidents.Description: A series of assaults by a gang of youths aged 16–20, apparently directed by local Legion commander John DeGrove, who turned up at the scenes, told Witnesses to leave, and sometimes joined in. Assailant Harry Stanfield, 19, told police DeGrove had told them to do it. DeGrove was questioned several times but never charged; a detective said the police force was "ninety percent American Legion."
incidents.Perpetrators: Youth gang; Legion commander John DeGrove
incidents.Law enforcement role: Police never charged DeGrove; detective said police had no control over the Legion
incidents.Source cited in text: Statement of Allan D. Weaver, July 5, 1941; A.M. Mellander letters, July 3 & 11, 1941; statements of Kadjzik, Nalepinski, Rose, Armstrong (June 28, 1941) and Mellander, Mesarik, Hare, Baumgartner, Buzalski, Barwig (Oct. 3, 1941); Harry Barwig, Oct. 16, 1941. ACLUP vol. 2328
incidents.Notes: Multiple incidents over four months; the author treats them as one series.

incidents.Description: A mob dragged and beat two Witness men while others threw stones and rotten fruit. Legion members were present directing the beating. Children around age twelve had collected decayed fruit that afternoon, which the writer took as proof the riot was planned.
incidents.Source cited in text: Letter to ACLU (author not visible), Oct. 22, 1940, ACLUP vol. 2230
incidents.Notes: Probably the same event as JW-61 (the mob that attacked the Witnesses' two attorneys after the Sept. 24, 1940 verdict). The chapter gives only the date of the letter.

incidents.Type of violence / persecution: Repeated harassment and assault; attempted forced flag salute
incidents.Description: A series of attacks by a mob of boys aged ten and up, backed by the town and urged on by local businessmen including A.B. Steelman, manager of the Hotel Corning. The boys tried to make Witnesses salute a large flag, then pelted them with water bags and clumps of dirt; one Witness was struck many times. Before this, a Legion member had ordered the Witnesses out of town.
incidents.Perpetrators: Boys; local businessmen (A.B. Steelman); Legion member
incidents.Source cited in text: Letter of Payne Creek Company of Jehovah's Witnesses to DOJ Civil Liberties Unit, Jan. 14, 1942, ACLUP vol. 2319

incidents.Type of violence / persecution: Expulsion order; threat of mob violence
incidents.Description: The police chief told Witnesses who had worked there for a year that they had to leave because they were about to be mobbed. He said he could not stop it because most of the businessmen were against them, and they would be "hurt and killed" if they stayed.
incidents.Source cited in text: Letter of Read A. Wilkinson to DOJ Civil Liberties Unit, Jan. 17, 1942, ACLUP vol. 2408

incidents.Place: Sandpoint (street in front of the Elks Building)
incidents.Description: The president of the Bonner County National Bank and three bank employees, all Elks Lodge members, attacked a Witness working in the street, kicking him and hitting him in the face as he walked past the American flag hanging in front of the Elks Building.
incidents.Perpetrators: Bank president and three bank employees (Elks members)
incidents.Source cited in text: Letter of Read A. Wilkinson, Jan. 17, 1942, ACLUP vol. 2408
incidents.Notes: About a month after JW-08.

incidents.Description: Emil Koch and his family were circulating petitions against the cancellation of the Witness convention at the Ohio State Fairgrounds. Bystander John Zeiler ordered them out of town "by the authority of the American Legion" and tore up a petition, and a crowd under his lead stopped their work. The police chief, saying he had "this bunch" behind him, told them to leave; the mob pushed them about a block to their car, threatening them.
incidents.Law enforcement role: Police chief sided with crowd and ordered them out
incidents.Source cited in text: Affidavit of Emil Koch, July 3, 1940, ACLUP vol. 2220

incidents.Type of violence / persecution: Arrests under anti-peddling ordinance; mob beating
incidents.Description: Six Witnesses were charged under an anti-peddling ordinance passed weeks earlier at the urging of a local Legion and VFW member. About 1,000 people gathered outside the courthouse. After the six pleaded not guilty, a local man rose in court to denounce Witnesses as un-American, invoking the VFW and Legion, to applause. Outside, members of the crowd beat the affiant until he was "hardly recognizable."
incidents.American Legion / veterans involved: Yes (Legion and VFW invoked; ordinance instigated by member)
incidents.Source cited in text: Affidavit of Ernest Miller, Jerome Fain, and Otto Bauer, Aug. 14, 1940, ACLUP vol. 2242

incidents.Description: Witnesses canvassing door to door on a Sunday morning were removed after the local American Legion asked the marshal to make them leave; the sheriff told them they were not wanted and they left. A local paper accused the Legion of "mob rule and violence"; Legionnaire W.K. Kathly replied that there were no threats.
incidents.Law enforcement role: Sheriff ordered them out at Legion request
incidents.Source cited in text: W.K. Kathly, "What Happened Sunday in Syracuse?" Syracuse Journal-Democrat, July 5, 1940
incidents.Notes: Kathly's letter disputes that violence occurred.

incidents.Description: Vigilantes seized 35 Witnesses from nearby Wheeling and took them to the American Legion Hall, where a Legion spokesman told them to leave because they did not salute the flag. About 60 people gathered and turned it into a mock hearing. A townsperson who defended their rights was asked if he was "one of them." The Witnesses were escorted out of town.
incidents.Source cited in text: Affidavit of R.L. Drummond, June 4, 1941, ACLUP vol. 2339
incidents.Notes: Victims came from Wheeling, WV (40.0640, -80.7209).

incidents.Description: A Snohomish insurance agent told Witness Edmond Perrenoud, of nearby Everett, that the Legion had discussed them at its last meeting and was "going to stop you."
incidents.Source cited in text: Edmond M. Perrenoud affidavit, July 8, 1940, ACLUP vol. 2249
incidents.Notes: First of three Snohomish incidents.

incidents.Type of violence / persecution: Threat of mob violence by police
incidents.Description: Police Chief O.D. Morse warned Perrenoud and other Witnesses to stop their work or be mobbed, saying he acted not for city officials but for an "outside source."
incidents.Source cited in text: Edmond M. Perrenoud affidavit, July 8, 1940, ACLUP vol. 2249

incidents.Description: After Legionnaire Noble Des Press harassed the Witnesses at work, the police chief arrested them. Mayor Chas Banworth said they were arrested because they did not salute the flag, named the Legion as the complainant (confirmed by Legionnaires Des Press and John Bird), told them to get out and stay out, and said the Legion would lynch them if they did not. He refused to hear their argument under Lovell v. Griffin.
incidents.Perpetrators: Legionnaires Noble Des Press and John Bird; police chief; Mayor Chas Banworth
incidents.Source cited in text: Edmond M. Perrenoud affidavit, July 8, 1940, ACLUP vol. 2249

incidents.Description: Witnesses Mr. Nichols and Mrs. Sprague were tried before a police judge for peddling without a license (no Guthrie attorney would take the case). When their attorney gave notice of appeal, two other Witnesses who came forward to post bond were immediately arrested and jailed.
incidents.Source cited in text: "Is This Germany Or Is This America?" affidavit, July 19, 1940, ACLUP vol. 2220

incidents.Description: Officers and Legionnaires rushed the Witnesses' attorney (not a Witness himself) and demanded he salute the flag, then shoved him, took his wallet, watch and keys, scattered his papers and jailed him. Officers said the Legion planned to tear down the jail that night. After midnight Police Chief Fred Streeter released him but refused him protection or a call to friends, and finally drove him to the nearby town of Coyle.
incidents.Law enforcement role: Officers took part; chief refused protection
incidents.Source cited in text: "Is This Germany Or Is This America?" affidavit, July 19, 1940, ACLUP vol. 2220
incidents.Notes: Attorney's name illegible in source. Released to Coyle, OK (35.9548, -97.2350).

incidents.Description: The police chief said anyone who refused to salute the flag ought to be investigated, and warned Witnesses that "patriotic Legionnaires" might come after them.
incidents.Source cited in text: Affidavit of John R. Barnes, July 15, 1940, ACLUP vol. 2220

incidents.Description: A carload of Legionnaires seized Witnesses by force, took them to the Legion Hall, questioned and threatened them, claiming the police had deputized them. The chief later denied it.
incidents.Source cited in text: Affidavit of John R. Barnes, July 15, 1940, ACLUP vol. 2220

incidents.Description: Other Orlando Witnesses reported that police picked them up and handed them over to the Legion at its hall.
incidents.Source cited in text: Affidavit of John R. Barnes, July 15, 1940, ACLUP vol. 2220

incidents.Description: Police Chief Ewell told J.W. Jones, who had distributed the Watchtower on street corners without trouble for most of 1942, that his work would not be allowed in Pascagoula.
incidents.Source cited in text: J.W. Jones affidavit, June 8, 1942, ACLUP vol. 2414
incidents.Notes: First of eight Pascagoula incidents against J.W. Jones.

incidents.Description: Legion commander L.L. Stigler and Deputy Sheriff Lee Byrd stopped Jones's street work, claimed they "represent the law," and ordered him to appear before the Legion post the next evening; Stigler warned it would go badly for him if his work was not on the square.
incidents.Perpetrators: Legion commander L.L. Stigler; Deputy Sheriff Lee Byrd
incidents.Source cited in text: J.W. Jones affidavit, June 8, 1942, ACLUP vol. 2414

incidents.Description: Before 30–35 Legionnaires, some drunk, with Stigler presiding, Harold Gautier cross-examined Jones harshly for nearly two hours while Jones suffered an angina attack. Some urged his arrest. After motions and a vote, Jones and others like him were ordered to stop all work within Post #160's defined "jurisdiction" or be arrested.
incidents.Source cited in text: J.W. Jones affidavit, June 8, 1942, ACLUP vol. 2414

incidents.Description: Stigler published an article in the Chronicle Star, Jackson County's leading paper, urging anyone exposed to Witness "propaganda" to call the police or the Legion and hold the Witness until someone came to arrest him.
incidents.Source cited in text: J.W. Jones affidavit, June 8, 1942, ACLUP vol. 2414

incidents.Description: The police chief arrested Jones for peddling without a license. Legionnaires then visited him in the county jail and said they had given him a chance to leave, that everyone must salute the flag, and that refusers would be put in concentration camps.
incidents.Source cited in text: J.W. Jones affidavit, June 8, 1942, ACLUP vol. 2414

incidents.Type of violence / persecution: Threat of beating by sheriff; protection refused
incidents.Description: A county highway patrolman alerted the sheriff to Jones's work, and the sheriff physically menaced him, called him a "dirty cur," threatened to beat him if he caught him alone, and said he was not worthy of protection because he would not salute the flag. The patrolman walked away when Jones asked for protection.
incidents.Law enforcement role: Sheriff was perpetrator; patrolman refused protection
incidents.Source cited in text: J.W. Jones affidavit, June 8, 1942, ACLUP vol. 2414

incidents.Description: A county patrolman stopped Jones and called the sheriff, whose office referred him to Stigler, who referred him to the Legion's "investigator" Gautier. Gautier advised watching Jones rather than arresting him while he studied the law on the case. (This patrolman was sympathetic to Jones.)
incidents.Source cited in text: J.W. Jones affidavit, June 8, 1942, ACLUP vol. 2414

incidents.Type of violence / persecution: Assault; forced into car; threats of beating
incidents.Description: Three hours after three Witnesses served the mayor and sheriff with notice that they would hold the city and county liable for failing to protect them, a small group of drunken Legionnaires assaulted Jones on a lonely road. Their leader gave him 24 hours to leave or be beaten "across a log," threatened to break every bone in his body, and forced Jones and his wife into their car, claiming authority from Post 160's 130 members. The sheriff's office said all deputies were away.
incidents.Geocode precision: Approximate (exact roadside not given; plotted at Pascagoula)
incidents.Source cited in text: J.W. Jones affidavit, June 8, 1942, ACLUP vol. 2414

incidents.Description: Brutal mob violence against Witnesses in Wyoming, described by Eleanor Roosevelt in her syndicated "My Day" column.
incidents.Notes: Town not named in this text. Other accounts generally place it in Rawlins, WY (41.7911, -107.2387); verify before using.

incidents.Type of violence / persecution: Mob attack led by deputy sheriff
incidents.Description: Deputy Sheriff William Catlette openly led a mob attack, which the author calls remarkably brutal and grotesque, in front of thousands of eyewitnesses. In 1942 he became the first and only law officer successfully prosecuted for anti-Witness violence, under Section 20 of the criminal code.
incidents.Notes: The incident date isn't given here; the case record (Catlette v. United States) dates it to June 29, 1940; verify.

incidents.Description: Under pressure, the Ohio State Fair Association canceled its contract for the Witnesses' national convention (July 24–29, 1940) at the Columbus fairgrounds, which also affected 30+ linked conventions. Witnesses' nationwide petition against it appears in dozens of affidavits from June–July 1940.
incidents.Notes: Not physical violence; included as institutional exclusion.

incidents.Description: Albert Stroebel was confronted on a friend's porch by three men who asked if he would salute the flag. When he declined they shouted "Nazi spy," beat him unconscious, dragged him to a service station and tried again to make him salute, while a crowd yelled for him to be strung up. A deputy sheriff jailed him and his father "to protect you," then took them to the sheriff's office in Prescott, where officials spent hours inspecting his literature, found nothing wrong, and released them after midnight.
incidents.Law enforcement role: Deputy jailed the victims; sheriff's office searched their literature
incidents.Source cited in text: Affidavit of Albert Stroebel (Flagstaff, AZ), June 26, 1940
incidents.Notes: Same day and town as JW-34.

incidents.Type of violence / persecution: Mob beating; dragging; expulsion; property burned
incidents.Description: Six cars surrounded the house where Roy Crabb and his brother were visiting, led by a car driven by local deputy sheriff Russell, who then drove away. About a dozen men dragged the brothers into the street, demanded they salute a U.S. flag, and beat, kicked and dragged them by their legs until they were semiconscious, then drove them out of town. The mob took their literature and phonographs, which were reportedly burned. One attacker was identified as Bud LaMar of Jerome.
incidents.Law enforcement role: Deputy sheriff led the convoy, then left
incidents.Source cited in text: Affidavit of Roy Crabb (Prescott, AZ), June 29, 1940
incidents.Notes: Same affiant as JW-04 (Winslow, AZ).

incidents.Description: After the Ash Fork attacks, the Witnesses asked for a deputy to go with them to identify the attackers. The under-sheriff agreed, but the next day Sheriff Robbins refused to send one, saying only that he would serve any warrants they swore out; Assistant District Attorney Frank backed him.
incidents.Law enforcement role: Sheriff refused to send a deputy
incidents.Notes: Follows from JW-33 and JW-34.

incidents.Description: Pulaski County Sheriff Roy Cadwell and Prosecuting Attorney Ed Cusick came to Millard Pemberton's trailer twice, the second time at 10:30 p.m. with about nine others. After hearing his records they said there was nothing wrong with them, but that because the family would not salute the flag they should be run out of the country, and both said they would give no protection.
incidents.Perpetrators: Sheriff Roy Cadwell; Prosecuting Attorney Ed Cusick; ~9 others
incidents.Law enforcement role: Sheriff and prosecutor were the perpetrators
incidents.Source cited in text: Affidavit of Millard H. Pemberton, July 4, 1940

incidents.Type of violence / persecution: Armed threats; gunfire at property; arson threat; expulsion
incidents.Description: Howard Shackley, Ted Spears and Clarence Quisenberry Jr. gave Pemberton 45 minutes to leave the county. When they returned Shackley shot ten holes in three of his tires; later they came back with gasoline to burn the trailer and Shackley drew a gun on him. At 8 a.m. Carl Brisch and five others said they would burn the trailer if the family was not gone by noon. The family left at 10:30 a.m. The sheriff refused protection and the state police, called twice, never came.
incidents.Perpetrators: Howard Shackley; Ted Spears; Clarence Quisenberry Jr.; Carl Brisch and five others
incidents.Law enforcement role: Sheriff refused protection; state police did not respond
incidents.Source cited in text: Affidavit of Millard H. Pemberton, July 4, 1940

incidents.Description: A mob of Legionnaires dragged Witnesses out of their cars in the Court House Square and beat them. Bystanders who tried to help, including a frail woman and her daughter, were also beaten. When the woman and her daughter asked the sheriff, a deputy and the town marshal for protection, the officers stood by and laughed.
incidents.Law enforcement role: Sheriff, deputy and town marshal watched and refused help
incidents.Source cited in text: Affidavit of John Q. Adams (Beaumont, TX), Oct. 30, 1940

incidents.Type of violence / persecution: Stalking; ambush attempts; family forced out
incidents.Description: The same mob had been trailing Witnesses and trying to ambush them, and forced one family to leave the county.
incidents.Source cited in text: Affidavit of John Q. Adams, Oct. 30, 1940

incidents.Description: Deputy Sheriff R.B. Gilbert warned his sister, Witness Mrs. Dave Stanford, that the American Legion would beat Witnesses to death if it caught them preaching, and that they could expect no protection from the law. The Jasper County sheriff said no Witness would ever see the inside of the Jasper jail but would be turned over to the mob.
incidents.Perpetrators: Deputy Sheriff R.B. Gilbert; Jasper County sheriff
incidents.Law enforcement role: Officers said they would hand Witnesses to the mob
incidents.Source cited in text: Affidavit of John Q. Adams, Oct. 30, 1940

incidents.Description: B.P. Jones, a Black Witness from Beaumont who had just performed a baptism for local Black residents, was forced into a car by a man with a shotgun and taken to a cemetery. The mob tied his hands, put a rope around his neck, and beat him with a wet rope and a pole cut from a tree, using racial slurs. They gave him three minutes to get his things and leave Jasper, then followed him 8 or 9 miles out of town.
incidents.Geocode precision: Approximate (cemetery not identified; plotted at Jasper)
incidents.Source cited in text: Affidavit of John Q. Adams, Oct. 30, 1940
incidents.Notes: The attack was both racial and anti-Witness.

incidents.Place: Rural Canadian County, just west of Union City
incidents.Type of violence / persecution: Armed threats; beating; forced flag salute; gunfire
incidents.Description: While Lee Bruton's group canvassed farmhouses, five men fixed a small U.S. flag to their car and said they would make them salute it, called them Germans who should be sent to Germany, and threatened to shoot them. As Bruton tried to start his car, two of the men hit him and broke his nose while a gun was fired around the car. The men cursed the law, said "We are the law," and boasted that the Canadian County sheriff had told them to do what they wanted.
incidents.Geocode precision: Approximate (rural area; plotted at Union City)
incidents.Source cited in text: Affidavit of Lee Bruton (Hinton, OK), Sept. 18, 1940

incidents.Type of violence / persecution: Arrest; beating by police; detention without charges
incidents.Description: Bond County Sheriff Cecil McCracken and deputies, including Clinton County Deputy Robert Hooker, stopped eight Witnesses distributing the Watchtower and arrested them. Edwin and Edgar Kircher were struck repeatedly on the way to the Bond County jail and beaten again there; Maynord Kircher was hit with a revolver butt. The officers were visibly drunk. The Witnesses were held about 16 hours without charges.
incidents.Perpetrators: Sheriff Cecil McCracken; Deputy Robert Hooker; deputies
incidents.Source cited in text: Affidavit of Edgar A. and Edwin M. Kircher, July 4, 1940

incidents.Type of violence / persecution: Assault in custody; threats; forced removal
incidents.Description: Deputy Hooker took Edgar Kircher and Truman Marietta to the Clinton County jail and beat them again to make them promise never to bring their literature into Carlyle or Clinton County, threatening to lead a mob against them. After a night and most of the next day in jail without charges, they were driven to about a mile from the Bond–Clinton county line and dumped.
incidents.Source cited in text: Affidavit of Edgar A. and Edwin M. Kircher, July 4, 1940

incidents.Place: Highway 127 near the Bond–Clinton county line
incidents.Description: As the released Witnesses walked home on Highway 127, the occupants of a brown car (whom the county officers had been seen waving to) and a second car took them down a side road and beat them to make them salute the flag.
incidents.Perpetrators: Occupants of two cars, apparently signaled by officers
incidents.Geocode precision: Approximate (point on IL-127 at county line)
incidents.Source cited in text: Affidavit of Edgar A. and Edwin M. Kircher, July 4, 1940

incidents.Description: Assistants of H.M.S. Dixon, who was arranging the Witnesses' convention in Jackson, were repeatedly arrested and released without charges.
incidents.Source cited in text: Letter of H.M.S. Dixon (Jackson, MS) to the Solicitor General

incidents.Type of violence / persecution: Seizure and destruction of property; break-in; threats
incidents.Description: About 50 men who said they represented the American Legion took several hundred dollars' worth of property from the convention office, saying it would be destroyed. The same day they forced their way into the tourist camp where Witnesses were living in leased trailers, took literature and Bibles, and threatened to remove them by force if they were not out of the state by 5 a.m. the next day.
incidents.Perpetrators: ~50 men claiming to represent the American Legion
incidents.Source cited in text: Letter of H.M.S. Dixon to the Solicitor General

incidents.Place: Jackson (camp on Pocahontas Road) to Vicksburg
incidents.Type of violence / persecution: Forced deportation across state line; property damaged
incidents.Description: A mob led by Major Birdsong, who ran a private detective agency in Jackson, entered the leased camp, put the Witnesses into cars by force, towed their trailers with wreckers across the Mississippi River at Vicksburg into Louisiana, and refused to let women and children stop for toilets or food. Dixon's trailer was badly damaged. Birdsong threatened the life of any of the men who returned to Mississippi, though several owned property there. The ACLU called it a federal crime, but the U.S. attorney sought no indictment.
incidents.Perpetrators: Mob led by Major Birdsong; Legionnaires
incidents.Law enforcement role: U.S. attorney declined to seek indictments
incidents.Source cited in text: Letter of H.M.S. Dixon to the Solicitor General
incidents.Notes: Route: Jackson → Vicksburg (32.3526, -90.8779) → Tallulah, LA. See JW-49.

incidents.Type of violence / persecution: Handover to police; ordered to move on; property impounded
incidents.Description: At Tallulah, Birdsong handed the Witnesses to the sheriff, who ordered them to move on, and left Dixon's trailer with the sheriff, who put it on the jail grounds. Legionnaires drove ahead, and in every town officers met them and ordered them on. Dixon got away at Monroe, LA.
incidents.Perpetrators: Sheriff at Tallulah; officers in other towns; Legionnaires
incidents.Law enforcement role: Sheriff and officers ordered them out
incidents.Source cited in text: Letter of H.M.S. Dixon to the Solicitor General
incidents.Notes: Dixon left the convoy at Monroe, LA (32.5093, -92.1193).

incidents.Description: Edwin Bobb and Richard Trask asked a York County deputy sheriff for protection against a planned attempt to break up their meeting. He shouted that they should not come to him or to any other deputies for protection, because the others were Legionnaires too.
incidents.Notes: First of the Kennebunk incidents (JW-50 to JW-57) that make up JW-02.

incidents.Description: The meeting went ahead without police protection, with the hall full of hostile men. A rock crashed through and narrowly missed Mrs. Bobb's head.

During a Sunday meeting and Bible study, rocks, fruit and garbage were thrown through the windows, breaking every front window while others smashed the back windows. After the Witnesses fled, the attackers broke down the doors and smashed all the furniture. The crowd below was estimated at about 2,000, including a few uniformed Salvation Army members.

A mob attacked the Kingdom Hall, smashing the front, the windows and even the walls. When attackers returned with armfuls of beer bottles, a shot was fired from the building and they fled. The next day a state policeman told the Witnesses their lives were in danger.
incidents.Law enforcement role: State police warned of danger but could not control it

incidents.Description: A large car swerved toward the hall's front doors, then circled in the road. When Mrs. Bobb went out to take the license number, the occupants tried to run her over.
incidents.Notes: The affidavit calls the next night June 7, but June 7, 1940 was itself a Friday, so this date may be off by a day.

incidents.Type of violence / persecution: Thrown rocks; tar-and-feather threat; protection refused
incidents.Description: A hail of rocks hit the back of the hall after a service meeting. The Witnesses could not get an officer, heard that a mob planned to tar and feather them, and wired the governor and the Maine attorney general for protection, but got no answer.
incidents.Law enforcement role: No officer available; governor and attorney general did not answer

incidents.Type of violence / persecution: Siege; exchange of fire; arrest of victims; death threats
incidents.Description: About eight cars circled the hall until 2:30 a.m., when three men got out and began throwing rocks. Shots were fired from inside the hall and two attackers were hospitalized. The state police then arrested the Witnesses; the father of one wounded man threatened the Bobbs in their cell. Police said the mob was so vicious their lives were "not worth a nickel" outside. Six Witnesses were charged with assault and attempted murder.
incidents.Law enforcement role: Police arrested the victims, not the attackers
incidents.Flag salute cited: Yes (threat to make Mrs. Bobb "salute something")
incidents.Notes: The ACLU says these events preceded the Kingdom Hall burning (JW-57).

incidents.Description: The Kingdom Hall was burned. Those charged with burning it were tried and all acquitted. Of the Witnesses charged after the June 9 shooting, one was convicted of assault with intent to kill (appealed), four were acquitted and one was awaiting trial.
incidents.Notes: Peters (pp. 9, 78–79) places the burning in the early hours of June 9, 1940, after a mob "led by American Legion boys, most of them drunk" gathered at the jail; see JW-83.

incidents.Type of violence / persecution: Assault on Witness; fatal shooting in self-defense claim
incidents.Description: A garage man threatened Witness Arthur F. Cox, who had offered to play him phonograph records, and hit him with a tire iron. In the scuffle Cox pulled a gun and shot him. Cox claimed self-defense but was convicted of murder; the case was on appeal.
incidents.Notes: Peters (p. 217): the man killed was garage owner and deputy sheriff Dean Pray, who chased Witnesses Arthur Cox and Kenneth Carr with a tire iron; Cox was convicted of murder on Oct. 1, 1940.

incidents.Type of violence / persecution: Arrest without warrant; jailing on inflated charges
incidents.Description: Six women were distributing literature door to door. When they refused the sheriff's demand to stop and to salute the flag, five were arrested without a warrant and charged with desecrating the flag. Because that carried only a $10 fine, a riotous conspiracy charge (a statute aimed at the Ku Klux Klan) was added against Grace Trent and Lucy McKee, with $3,000 bond each; they stayed in jail until Aug. 20. Three others, under great pressure, pleaded guilty and got suspended sentences on promising to stop.

incidents.Type of violence / persecution: Criminal conviction for refusing flag salute
incidents.Description: Grace Trent (70) and Lucy McKee (in her fifties) were tried for riotous conspiracy, effectively for refusing to salute the flag. A change of venue was refused, Watch Tower books and the Bible were put in evidence, and the assistant prosecutor made an inflammatory speech. They were convicted and on Sept. 24 sentenced to two to ten years in Indiana State Prison, and not released on bond until early December.
incidents.Source cited in text: Statement of a local attorney; ACLU narrative

incidents.Description: After the verdict a mob, including the local American Legion commander and hundreds of others, attacked the defense attorneys outside the courthouse. One was marched half a mile and beaten; the other was pelted with objects and fell in the gutter expecting to be killed. Eggs had been thrown even before the verdict, and police made no effort to protect the lawyers.
incidents.Notes: Probably the same event as JW-06.

incidents.Description: Seventy-five deputy sheriffs were sworn in from local organizations, many from the American Legion, to stop the circulation of Witness literature.
incidents.Perpetrators: Fayette County sheriff; Legionnaires as deputies

incidents.Description: Six Witnesses were arrested under the state sedition act for supposedly advocating another form of government ("theocracy") and held for weeks. They were freed only after Witness counsel Hayden Covington asked a three-judge federal court for an injunction; the court told the state to stop using the sedition law against Witnesses.
incidents.Notes: The ACLU says this was the only place where federal jurisdiction was successfully invoked against local officials.

incidents.Description: One of three communities where, in October 1940, the Justice Department ordered U.S. attorneys to put evidence against local officials and citizens before grand juries.
incidents.Notes: The incident isn't described in the pamphlet.

incidents.Description: One of three communities where, in October 1940, the Justice Department ordered U.S. attorneys to put evidence against local officials and citizens before grand juries.
incidents.Notes: The incident isn't described in the pamphlet.

incidents.Description: A Jackson Daily News editorial praised the forced removal of the Witnesses' camp on Pocahontas Road as the "proper disposal" of a threat, and said Jackson had no room for anyone who would not salute the flag.
incidents.Notes: Comments on JW-48.

incidents.Description: Courts ordered several Witness children removed from their homes to state institutions over refusal to salute the flag.

Nineteen Witness children were expelled from school for refusing the flag salute. A local judge arranged a compromise letting them return; it fell through, and they were eventually excused from the exercises altogether.
A Georgia town required permits to distribute literature and refused them to Witnesses. The U.S. Supreme Court struck the ordinance down.
incidents.Notes: The pamphlet doesn't name the town; this is Lovell v. City of Griffin (1938).

incidents.Description: Witnesses were prosecuted under a Connecticut law banning door-to-door religious canvassing without a permit. The U.S. Supreme Court struck the law down, upholding their right to canvass, sell tracts and play records on request.
incidents.Notes: The pamphlet doesn't name the place; this is Cantwell v. Connecticut (1940), which arose in New Haven.

incidents.Type of violence / persecution: Arrest; mob beating; abduction; hanging threat
incidents.Description: A constable arrested John Golinie and Frank Kikosicsky for distributing literature without a permit. At the town fire siren, a mob of 50 to 100 or more beat the remaining Witnesses, dragging some through the streets. In a second wave, men in the town fire truck smashed a car's windows with axes, beat Witnesses who would not salute the flag, loaded them into the truck and said they would hang them. State police intercepted the truck. Police held the injured Witnesses for hours before they could get treatment.
incidents.Perpetrators: Mob of 50–100+, incl. men on the town fire truck; constable
incidents.Law enforcement role: Constable arrested Witnesses; police held victims; state police intervened
incidents.Source cited in text: Peters, Judging Jehovah's Witnesses (2000); accounts of G.C. Flick, William Comodor, Walter Vrusk
incidents.Notes: The two arrested Witnesses had been accosted in Imperial a few days earlier.

incidents.Description: Rioters in two fire trucks hosed down John Kikosicsky Jr.'s house, stoned out the windows, then broke in and wrecked it while the family escaped through a basement window.
incidents.Perpetrators: Drunken rioters with two fire trucks
incidents.Law enforcement role: Family had to summon police after escaping
incidents.Notes: Same night as the Imperial street attack.

incidents.Description: About 40 Witnesses canvassing house to house, including 11-year-old Lillian Gobitas, were mobbed by a crowd Lillian put near 1,000. Police took them into cells in the fire house while the mob tried to break down the door; a girl punched Lillian. Police kept the men; women and children were released.
incidents.Source cited in text: Peters, Judging Jehovah's Witnesses (2000); recollection of Lillian Gobitas Klose

incidents.Description: Third-grader Carleton Nicholls was expelled for refusing the pledge. Supporter Edward H. James was jailed after a protest in the boy's classroom. The state's highest court upheld the expulsion in 1937.
After they stopped saluting, Lillian and Billy Gobitas and Edmund Wasliewski were pelted with pebbles by other children on the way to and from school and taunted with "Here comes Jehovah!"

At Superintendent Charles Roudabush's urging, the school board adopted a flag-salute rule and expelled Lillian and William Gobitas and Edmund Wasliewski. Families feared the children would be sent to reform school, and the Witnesses set up their own Kingdom School.
incidents.Perpetrators: Minersville school board; Supt. Charles Roudabush
incidents.Notes: Led to Minersville School District v. Gobitis (1940).

incidents.Description: A crowd of 400 forced three Witnesses out of town after they tried to distribute tracts and play recordings. A wire story falsely called them Nazi agents.
incidents.Flag salute cited: Implied (story claimed they mocked the flag)

incidents.Description: About 60 Witnesses arriving for a zone assembly were herded by sheriff's deputies to the jail, lectured on Americanism and held overnight.

incidents.Place: Odessa to the Ector County line
incidents.Type of violence / persecution: Beatings by officers; forced expulsion march
incidents.Description: Sheriff Reeder Webb struck Witness Virgil Walker and a deputy slapped a 61-year-old man. About 75 Witnesses were loaded onto a flatbed truck and driven to the county line, followed by hundreds of cars, then forced to walk four or five miles along a railroad bed in extreme heat with the mob following; some collapsed.
incidents.Perpetrators: Sheriff Reeder Webb; deputies; mob in hundreds of cars
incidents.Source cited in text: Peters, Judging Jehovah's Witnesses (2000); accounts of H.C. Beattie, Virgil Walker
incidents.Notes: The march ended near Midland at a Witness's farm.

incidents.Type of violence / persecution: Kingdom Hall ransacked; Witnesses driven out
incidents.Description: The Witnesses' Kingdom Hall in Saco was ransacked and the Witnesses were driven out of town, after which they moved to Kennebunk.

Gertrude and Edwin Bobb were followed and taunted while canvassing (May 20) and found their car vandalized (May 21). Friends warned that local Legionnaires planned to attack the Kingdom Hall. On Memorial Day, cars and carloads of Boy Scouts circled the hall all day yelling "Jehovah!"
incidents.Law enforcement role: County attorney, state police and governor gave no protection
incidents.Source cited in text: Peters, Judging Jehovah's Witnesses (2000); account of Gertrude Bobb
incidents.Notes: Precedes ACLU incidents JW-53 to JW-56.

incidents.Type of violence / persecution: Mob attack; office sacked; book burning
incidents.Description: After two National Guard officers claimed to have uncovered subversion, a huge crowd mobbed two Witnesses, sacked their office and burned hundreds of tracts in a public bonfire. A police officer called it the worst thing that ever happened in Sanford.
incidents.Source cited in text: Peters, Judging Jehovah's Witnesses (2000); ACLU report

incidents.Description: After the shooting at the Kingdom Hall, hundreds of villagers, "led by American Legion boys, most of them drunk", converged on the jail, then ransacked and set fire to the Kingdom Hall twice and burned the Witnesses' belongings in the street. A Witness man and woman from Biddeford were roughed up and dumped at the town line. The six arrested Witnesses were held on $5,000 bail each.
incidents.Perpetrators: Mob of hundreds led by drunk Legionnaires
incidents.Law enforcement role: Police moved prisoners to county jail; arsonists later acquitted
incidents.Source cited in text: Peters, Judging Jehovah's Witnesses (2000); Boston Globe; John Haynes Holmes
incidents.Notes: Adds detail to JW-56 and JW-57.

incidents.Type of violence / persecution: Home stoned; attempted tarring and feathering
incidents.Description: Shouting "salute the flag," a mob stoned the apartment of Witness John Anthony and his two daughters, dragged him from bed and prepared to tar and feather him before police intervened.
The same mob stoned the bungalow of Witness Benjamin Jariz, dragged him outside and beat him. His wife reportedly suffered a heart attack at a neighbor's home.

incidents.Type of violence / persecution: Mob attack on home (mistaken identity); shooting
incidents.Description: Rioters hunting "Fifth Columnists" stoned the home of Clarence Grant, a Navy Yard worker wrongly thought to be a Witness, even after he offered to salute. He fired a warning shot that wounded two teenage rioters and was not charged.
incidents.Law enforcement role: State police captain blamed the mob
incidents.Notes: The victim was not a Witness.

incidents.Description: Police and members of the American Legion expelled a small band of Witness evangelists from town.
incidents.Notes: Precedes the June 16 riot (JW-01), which Peters dates to June 16, 1940.

incidents.Description: About 50 rioters broke up a Bible study when the Witnesses refused to salute the flag, destroying desks, chairs, typewriters, literature and records. Two Montgomery County officers, whose headquarters stood across the street, watched "with arms folded." Ten residents were later arrested, Police Chief Charles Orne was dismissed, and the two officers were fined.
incidents.Law enforcement role: Two officers watched; chief later fired
incidents.Source cited in text: Peters, Judging Jehovah's Witnesses (2000); Washington Post

incidents.Description: State trooper Bernard McLaughlin took Witnesses C.A. Cecil and Stanley Jones into custody. Legionnaires Lee Reese, Deputy Martin Catlette and Louis Baber joined the questioning, called them Fifth Columnists, cited a recent Oklahoma mobbing, and said the Legion would "handle the matter" if they did not leave.
incidents.Perpetrators: Trooper Bernard McLaughlin; Legionnaires Lee Reese, Martin Catlette, Louis Baber
incidents.Law enforcement role: Trooper detained them; deputy threatened them
incidents.Source cited in text: Peters, Judging Jehovah's Witnesses (2000); account of C.A. Cecil
incidents.Notes: The next day's castor-oil attack is JW-31; Peters reports Catlette was fined $1,000 and jailed a year, and Police Chief Bert Stewart was fined $250.

incidents.Description: War veterans planned to break up a Witness Bible study by mob violence. Police intervened at the last minute but then jailed and fined Witnesses rather than the veterans.
incidents.Law enforcement role: Police jailed and fined the intended victims
incidents.Source cited in text: Peters, Judging Jehovah's Witnesses (2000); Rev. Frederick L. Gibson

incidents.Description: Twenty Witnesses collecting petition signatures were assaulted and jailed; those who came to post bail were jailed too, and all were held incommunicado. The head of the local American Legion post threatened mob violence at the station and was not arrested.
incidents.Source cited in text: Peters, Judging Jehovah's Witnesses (2000); letter of Oliver Siebenlist

incidents.Description: Police barred a planned Bible study and prohibited all assembly or activity of Jehovah's Witnesses in the entire county.
S.A. Senk and Ray Pillars were told to leave town; Pillars was taken outside town and beaten until his head was bruised and bleeding. Police refused to investigate.
incidents.Source cited in text: Peters, Judging Jehovah's Witnesses (2000); letter of S.A. Senk

incidents.Description: Members of the local Witness company reported harassment by a Catholic priest, war veterans, a marshal, a city councilman and a woman who ran through the streets denouncing them.
incidents.Source cited in text: Peters, Judging Jehovah's Witnesses (2000); complaint of Mrs. J.C. Kantz

incidents.Description: Two men posing as fellow Witnesses lured Albert Walkenhorst from his home to a grove of trees and castrated him. He wrote of the attack from his bed at Lutheran Hospital in Norfolk.
incidents.Geocode precision: Approximate (home location not given; plotted at Norfolk)

incidents.Description: Men armed with guns, sticks, blackjacks and pipe dragged Witnesses from their cars, beat them and left some in a ditch.
incidents.Source cited in text: Peters, Judging Jehovah's Witnesses (2000); ACLU, Jehovah's Witnesses and the War (1942)

incidents.Description: Witness J.B. Good was jailed in Marianna (photograph in Peters).
With police looking on, vigilantes broke up a Witness Bible study and drove the Witnesses out of town.
incidents.Source cited in text: Peters, Judging Jehovah's Witnesses (2000); ACLU Southern California branch

incidents.Description: Police Sergeant Charles Ellis assaulted Witness August Schmidt in his home, on the way to the station and inside it. Ellis was indicted on two counts, convicted on one and fined $100.
incidents.Source cited in text: Peters, Judging Jehovah's Witnesses (2000); ACLU Southern California branch

incidents.Description: A group of Witnesses was mobbed.
incidents.Source cited in text: Peters, Judging Jehovah's Witnesses (2000); Ohio League for Constitutional Rights

incidents.Description: Several dozen men, including two sheriff's deputies, confronted Witness Reginald Bourne and his wife and baby at their trailer; one carried gasoline to burn it, and a Methodist minister held them back. Sheriff Riley Nelson then pressed Bourne to leave, and the family fled to Omaha.
incidents.Perpetrators: Several dozen men incl. two deputies
incidents.Law enforcement role: Deputies in the mob; sheriff pushed victim out
incidents.Source cited in text: Peters, Judging Jehovah's Witnesses (2000); Iowa Civil Liberties Union

incidents.Description: The Legion's George Hart Post resolved that no Witness could distribute literature or play recordings in Harrisburg or the surrounding territory. On June 23, Deputy Sheriff and post commander Jack Edwards warned Witness Helen Jordan that the Legion would "get" the Witnesses.
incidents.Perpetrators: American Legion George Hart Post; Deputy Jack Edwards
incidents.Source cited in text: Peters, Judging Jehovah's Witnesses (2000); complaint to Solicitor General Biddle

incidents.Description: A Legion-organized boycott forced Witness Duncan Felts out of his Texaco station, and a Witness lost her job of 14 years at a local bank because its directors feared a boycott.
Under Legion pressure, miner Cecil Bevins's union card was revoked, his coworkers refused to work with him, and he was fired.
Deputy Sheriff and Legion commander Jack Edwards arrested Cecil Bevins at home for disturbing the peace, and a justice of the peace convicted him.

After weeks of harassment, a mob of more than a dozen men led by acting mayor Hill Everett seized the Witnesses' magazines, bags and literature and burned them in the street, then ordered them out of town. Sheriff Elmo Richie and Deputy Frank Bunch refused protection; the U.S. attorney declined to prosecute.
incidents.Perpetrators: Mob led by acting mayor Hill Everett
incidents.Source cited in text: Peters, Judging Jehovah's Witnesses (2000); ACLU (Clifford Forster)

incidents.Description: Police and Legionnaires stopped two Witnesses and took them to Mayor Ross Castle, who ordered them to stop proselytizing until the local Legion post cleared them.
incidents.Notes: Precedes the June 19–20 arrests (JW-59).

incidents.Description: After Judge G. Edwin Johnson barred him from consulting his clients, Witness attorney Victor Schmidt and his wife were followed by a cursing mob and chased out of town by 15 to 20 cars.
incidents.Source cited in text: Peters, Judging Jehovah's Witnesses (2000); Victor Schmidt

incidents.Description: Police Chief William Traylor and the county sheriff arrested all 75 visiting Witnesses, men, women and children, and charged them with riotous conspiracy and criminal syndicalism. Bail was set at $225,000 for the group, and a federal court refused an injunction.
incidents.Perpetrators: Police Chief William Traylor; Fayette County sheriff
incidents.Law enforcement role: Police and sheriff made the arrests

incidents.Description: Police arrested seven Witnesses for "desecrating the Sabbath" by going door to door. Four were convicted on Jan. 4, 1941; the Iowa Supreme Court reversed.
Four young Witnesses were arrested for proselytizing. When Witness attorney Victor Blackwell came to post bail, the city judge brandished a pistol and threatened to kill him if he ever returned.

incidents.Type of violence / persecution: Seizure of literature; assault; threats by mayor
incidents.Description: Mayor and Legion commander L.O. Smith signed the sedition warrants, seized Witnesses' literature, physically abused them and promised they would be mobbed. Officials confiscated a shipment of Bibles; bail was $10,000 each; a local attorney who took the case was threatened into dropping it.
incidents.Perpetrators: Mayor L.O. Smith; city attorney W.L. Rose
incidents.Source cited in text: Peters, Judging Jehovah's Witnesses (2000); letters of Dorothy Carr; Victor Schmidt
incidents.Notes: Adds detail to JW-63.

incidents.Description: The city enacted an ordinance against language or literature "calculated to cause a breach of the peace," later copied by Muskogee to suppress Witness proselytizing.

Pressed by the veterans' Americanism Club, the council passed Ordinance 1533. Police then arrested John Lynch and 39 other Witnesses 204 times in seven months; all but ten arrests ended in fines of $10 to $19.95. A federal court enjoined enforcement in Jan. 1942.
One of several towns where Witnesses had to seek federal injunctions against local interference with their work.
One of several towns where Witnesses had to seek federal injunctions against local interference with their work.
One of several towns where Witnesses had to seek federal injunctions against local interference with their work.
One of several towns where Witnesses had to seek federal injunctions against local interference with their work.
One of several towns where Witnesses had to seek federal injunctions against local interference with their work.
incidents.Notes: No Pennsylvania town of this name could be pinned down; may be a township.

incidents.Description: One of several towns where Witnesses had to seek federal injunctions against local interference with their work.
One of several towns where Witnesses had to seek federal injunctions against local interference with their work.

A week after the town council barred unapproved meetings in the park, about 25 veterans attacked a Witness meeting there; in nearly an hour of fighting, about 30 people were hurt by fists, pop bottles, clubs and brass knuckles.
incidents.Source cited in text: Peters, Judging Jehovah's Witnesses (2000); Des Moines Register

incidents.Description: Sheriff Lewis Johnson deputized nearly 200 men who, with state patrolmen, sealed every road into town to keep Witnesses out, with the backing of the mayor and Iowa's attorney general. An appeals court later ruled the blockade unconstitutional.
incidents.Perpetrators: Warren County Sheriff Lewis Johnson; ~200 deputies; Mayor Lo Goode

incidents.Description: Daniel Morgan's sons were expelled from high school for not saluting. When he refused to pressure them, his boss at the state Motor Vehicle Department charged him with insubordination and he was fired, though he was a wounded World War I veteran.
incidents.Perpetrators: School authorities; NJ Motor Vehicle Dept.

incidents.Description: After questioning him on the flag salute, state prison officials refused Daniel Morgan a job, and the Bergen County Freeholders refused to appoint him bridge attendant solely because he would not salute. A court reversed the county's refusal.
incidents.Perpetrators: NJ prison officials; Bergen County Freeholders

incidents.Description: After Pearl Harbor, union coworkers refused to work with Witness Paul Schmidt, hung a flag at his station and warned him to expect "even death." The company fired him, his son Bernard and five other Witnesses. The federal FEPC ordered them rehired in late 1942.
After postal clerk Helge Peterson spoke against a school flag-salute rule, the Legion's Rex Ish Post demanded his removal through their congressman, and the Postmaster General had him fired.
incidents.Perpetrators: American Legion Rex Ish Post; Postmaster General

incidents.Type of violence / persecution: School expulsion; Klan picketing; business lost
incidents.Description: Sixth-grader Dorothy Leoles was expelled for not saluting. The Ku Klux Klan's Buckhead Klavern then picketed her Greek-born father's hat-cleaning shop until he was forced to sell it.
incidents.Perpetrators: Atlanta school authorities; KKK Buckhead Klavern

incidents.Description: Henry Hopper and eight other Witnesses were arrested under an Illinois law against literature exposing a creed to contempt, and about a week later were convicted and fined $50 each.
Relief administrator Hugh Edwards refused the disabled Henry Hopper's family its grocery order and clothing, saying they would get no relief until Hopper saluted the flag.
Paul Hopper and James and Marjorie Baugher were expelled for refusing the pledge and salute; the school board refused to reconsider.
Fred Bleich's six children were suspended from public schools for not saluting; the Florida Supreme Court upheld the suspensions in 1939.

incidents.Type of violence / persecution: School expulsion; children committed to reformatory
incidents.Description: Roland, Loraine and Loretta Lefebvre (15, 12 and 10) were expelled. When their parents taught them at home, the children were charged as delinquents and committed to the State Industrial School in Manchester until age 21. The state supreme court reversed, but the school refused to readmit them in Sept. 1941.
Nine-year-old Doris Jones was expelled for not saluting and charged as a delinquent.
Eight-year-old Anson Reed was adjudged a delinquent for resisting flag-salute ceremonies; an appeals court reversed in May 1941.
Three of William Johnson's children were expelled and found guilty as "habitual school offenders," facing commitment to a county training school; the state's highest court reversed in 1941.

incidents.Type of violence / persecution: School expulsion; children made wards of state
incidents.Description: Children of the Bolling, Fuller, Grittman and Parr families were expelled and charged as delinquents; a judge made the Bolling children wards of the state. The state supreme court reversed in 1943.
Rep. Earle Byrne introduced a bill to fine or jail parents who taught children not to salute; it died in committee after ACLU opposition.
After their daughter Grace was expelled, Charles and Hilda Sandstrom were convicted of unlawfully keeping her out of school; an appeals court reversed.
After Mario and Josephine Latrecchia were expelled, their parents were convicted as disorderly persons; New Jersey's supreme court set the convictions aside in 1942.

After Thelma (11) and Wayne (9) Davis were expelled, their parents E.V. and Naomi Davis were convicted of contributing to delinquency by teaching them not to salute; Arizona's supreme court upheld the convictions in 1942.
A superior court judge questioned Kathleen Cory about the flag and the war and transferred custody of her two children to her ex-husband because of her Witness beliefs; an appeals court reversed.
Witnesses were prosecuted under municipal ordinances restricting distribution of literature; the Supreme Court struck them down in Schneider v. New Jersey (1939).
incidents.Notes: Peters names only the case; Schneider arose in Irvington, NJ.

incidents.Description: House Resolution 28, "Declaring Open Season on Jehovah's Witnesses," called their "extermination" meritorious and a duty of citizens. It died in committee.

The legislature passed and Gov. Paul Johnson signed Chapter 178, banning teaching that tended to create refusal to salute the flag; the ACLU said it virtually outlawed the Witnesses. The Supreme Court struck it down in Taylor v. Mississippi (1943).
Louisiana enacted a wartime measure similar to Mississippi's Chapter 178.
Otto and Roxie Mills were arrested under Chapter 178 for distributing a Witness tract, convicted and sentenced to up to ten years; the state supreme court reversed in Jan. 1943.

Police and deputies arrested R.E. Taylor and his wife in McComb and drove them to Magnolia, where the district attorney berated them and offered to fight. Five vigilantes then took turns threatening them and ordered them out of the county; Taylor said he was "run off by a mob."
incidents.Perpetrators: Police; deputies; district attorney; five vigilantes
incidents.Source cited in text: Peters, Judging Jehovah's Witnesses (2000); letter of R.E. Taylor

incidents.Description: The county attorney and sheriff searched the Taylors' rooms, seized literature, Bibles and phonographs and jailed them under Chapter 178. Taylor was convicted and faced up to ten years; the U.S. Supreme Court reversed in Taylor v. Mississippi (1943).
Clem Cummings was convicted under Chapter 178 for distributing the Witness book Children; reversed with Taylor (1943).

incidents.Type of violence / persecution: Police raid; property destroyed; book burning
incidents.Description: Police Chief Bill Owens and two officers broke up a Bible study in a Witness home, threatened mob violence, ordered the Witnesses out of town, smashed a phonograph and a 14-part recorded lecture and burned them with the literature.
incidents.Perpetrators: Police Chief Bill Owens; two officers
incidents.Source cited in text: Peters, Judging Jehovah's Witnesses (2000); letter of Betty Benoit

incidents.Description: Owens told Witnesses Betty Benoit and Violet Babin he would not protect them from vigilantes and twice persuaded landlords to evict them.

Benoit and Babin were arrested under Chapter 178, partly for a Consolation issue quoting a newspaper editorial against Gobitis, and warned that bond would be set unpayably high if they kept working. Benoit was convicted; reversed in 1943.

School attendance officer George Perkins confronted Sarah Prince on the street while her nine-year-old niece Betty Simmons distributed magazines; Prince was convicted under the child-labor law, and the Supreme Court upheld it (Prince v. Massachusetts, 1944).

Walter Chaplinsky was convicted of peddling without a license and chose 40 days in jail over leaving town. A jail official punched him on arrival "to show you who is boss," and he was made to pull a cultivator like a draft animal.
incidents.Source cited in text: Peters, Judging Jehovah's Witnesses (2000); Walter Chaplinsky

incidents.Description: After about 90 Witnesses held a single-file "information march" downtown, five (Willis Cox, Walter Chaplinsky, John Konides, Arvid Moody, Oliva Paquette) were convicted of parading without a license; the Supreme Court upheld it in Cox v. New Hampshire (1941).
After complaints about his preaching, City Marshal James Bowering took Chaplinsky into custody and warned him not to cause a disturbance.

incidents.Type of violence / persecution: Mob beating; arrest of victim; imprisonment
incidents.Description: Former VFW commander William Bowman lunged at Chaplinsky with a flagpole, and a crowd of veterans and mill workers beat him into the gutter; a deputy sheriff joined in. Police roughly hauled him off and arrested him, not the attackers, for calling the marshal a "fascist." His sentence was raised to six months, which he served on a prison farm, including six weeks in solitary.
incidents.Perpetrators: William Bowman; Robert Downing; Deputy Ralph Dunlap; crowd of ~50
incidents.Law enforcement role: Deputy joined attack; police arrested victim
incidents.Source cited in text: Peters, Judging Jehovah's Witnesses (2000); trial testimony
incidents.Notes: Led to Chaplinsky v. New Hampshire (1942).

incidents.Description: Patrolman Bert Power arrested Witness John Douglas when he tried to preach in Central Square; he was charged with disorderly conduct and abusive language.
Chaplinsky was punched in the face while proselytizing. Earlier that week youths deflated his tires and threatened to tip his car over if he returned.
incidents.Source cited in text: Peters, Judging Jehovah's Witnesses (2000); Rochester Courier

incidents.Description: Chaplinsky was convicted of disturbing the peace; the judge called Witnesses "a dirty bunch of murderers" and said "I despise you and your organization."
Rosco Jones, an African American Witness, was convicted for selling literature without paying the $10 annual peddler's license fee (Jones v. Opelika).
Witnesses were convicted under a $25-per-quarter peddler's license tax (consolidated in Jones v. Opelika).
Witnesses were convicted under peddler's license fees of $2.50 a day to $25 a month (consolidated in Jones v. Opelika).
Two Witnesses were convicted for selling literature without a license (Busey v. District of Columbia).
Witnesses were prosecuted under an ordinance banning distribution of handbills; reversed in Jamison v. Texas (1943).
A Witness was prosecuted under a permit ordinance; reversed in Largent v. Texas (1943).
Eight Witnesses were convicted under a canvassing license tax; reversed in Murdock v. Pennsylvania (1943). Witnesses also sued to stop the city's enforcement (Douglas v. Jeannette).
A Witness was convicted under an ordinance forbidding leaflet distributors to ring doorbells; reversed in Martin v. Struthers (1943).

Under a state Board of Education rule that quoted Gobitis, more than six children of the Barnette, Stull and McClure families were expelled; some parents were prosecuted. Led to West Virginia v. Barnette (1943).
incidents.Notes: Fox (Arkansas essays, p. 166) also notes parents prosecuted.

incidents.Description: William Estep was expelled for refusing the pledge and finished his schooling at a Witness Kingdom School in Gates, PA.

The draft board denied Estep's ministerial exemption; its clerk J.W. McNutt refused to file his affidavits and held up his appeal for nearly two years. Estep was convicted in late 1944 for refusing induction; reversed in Estep v. U.S. (1946).
After his draft board denied him a ministerial exemption, Louis Smith was seized at home without a warrant by a magistrate and two deputies (paid $30 by his father) and taken to Fort Jackson.

When Smith refused a uniform, soldiers stripped and forcibly dressed him, and he was held four days in the stockade's "black box" without clothes or food. He was later convicted under the draft law; reversed in Estep v. U.S. (1946).
Robert Deysher was convicted under the draft law for failing to report to a Civilian Public Service camp, the first of 45 Witnesses sent to Danbury prison that year.

incidents.Place: Queens to Camp Upton, Long Island
incidents.Description: Brooklyn Witness Frank Moncada, refusing the oath and flag salute at a Queens induction station, was carried crying into an army truck by grinning soldiers and taken to Camp Upton, then to Fort Jay for psychiatric evaluation. Released after ACLU protests.

Soldiers, two of them sergeants, doused Witness Ernie Strobel with hot water and beat and kicked him unconscious, threatening to kill him, then paraded him before other Witnesses as a warning. The War Department called his account false and put him in the stockade.
Herbert Weatherbee was physically abused, then court-martialed for refusing to salute the flag and sentenced to life at hard labor.

incidents.Type of violence / persecution: School expulsion; police destruction of property
incidents.Description: Harold Marsh was expelled for not saluting; vigilantes threatened Grace Marsh and Violet Babin. Police shoved them from a doorway, smashed their phonographs against a tree, broke their records, tore up their Bibles and literature and burned it all.
incidents.Source cited in text: Peters, Judging Jehovah's Witnesses (2000); Grace Marsh

incidents.Description: At a Baptist minister's urging, Grace and Herbert Marsh were arrested for trespassing and held nearly two weeks in a bedbug-infested cell until she caught pneumonia; vigilante threats drove them from town. Charges were later dismissed.
Deputy A.I. Chatham twice took Grace Marsh and Aileen Stephens into custody in the Gulf Shipbuilding company town, and company executive E.B. Peebles threatened them with arrest.
Witnesses were arrested again and again for trespassing, with rising bail and longer jail stays. Six were convicted on Jan. 27, 1944; reversed in Marsh v. Alabama (1946).
A Witness was convicted for holding a meeting in a city park without a permit; upheld in Poulos v. New Hampshire (1953).

Rosco Jones's wife was arrested for distributing literature. When he protested, police held him by his arms and legs, kicked him in the stomach and ribs and beat him over the head with a bicycle tire.
incidents.Source cited in text: Peters, Judging Jehovah's Witnesses (2000); Rosco Jones

incidents.Type of violence / persecution: Relief made conditional on flag salute
incidents.Description: Commissary clerk Nell Cooper confronted Witness Joe Johnson as he drew commodities for his large family and asked him to "prove" himself by saluting the flag; clerks were sworn not to give relief to anyone not a "loyal American citizen." He refused and spoke about the flag.

On Cooper's complaint, with Legion Post 117 commander Lawrence Exum signing the prosecution bond, Johnson was arrested under the 1919 flag statute. A justice-of-the-peace trial in Eli Jordan's living room, with Legion "hot-heads" outside, fined him $60 and gave him 30 days.
incidents.Perpetrators: Treadwell-Allen American Legion Post 117; JP court
incidents.Source cited in text: Fox (2016); interview with ex-deputy Howard Hensley

incidents.Description: The brother of a commissary clerk, an Army soldier, and others asked a local lawyer about seizing Johnson by force and taking him to Little Rock to be court-martialed; the lawyer told them it would be kidnapping.
incidents.Source cited in text: Fox (2016); trial testimony of Ogle Horton

incidents.Description: After a hung jury in Aug. 1941, Johnson was retried and convicted of publicly showing contempt for the flag, fined $50 and jailed 24 hours. The Arkansas Supreme Court affirmed on June 8, 1942, citing Gobitis.

other.Description: The San Francisco Vigilance Committee (first formed 1851, revived 1856) publicly hanged four criminals and took effective control of the city.
other.Targets: Alleged criminals (mainly Australian); political target the Irish-Catholic Democratic machine

other.Description: A Law and Order Committee judge stabbed a Vigilance Committee member during a botched arrest. The committee held back from executing him for fear of federal intervention.
other.Perpetrators: Law and Order Committee judge (stabbing); Vigilance Committee (arrest)
other.Notes: The judge isn't named in the text.
